title: White House rolls out AI funding — and signals a new era for US science
excerpt: Chief US science adviser calls for a shakeup in funding while handing out grants to accelerate research with AI.
content_html:
Washington DC

It was a big week for science in the administration of US President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, the president’s chief science adviser, Michael Kratsios, release a report called Science: A New Golden Age that proposes substantial changes to federally funded research. The next day saw him help to unveil some of the first winners of research grants from the Genesis Mission, the administration’s flagship artificial-intelligence initiative.

For the past year and a half, the Republican-led administration has made headlines for attempting to cut funding for US science that it disfavours. This week’s events are notable because they move forward the science that it does favour — in particular, AI.

Trump has big AI and quantum ambitions: this scientist’s job is to make them reality

Some 5,000 teams applied for funding from the Genesis Mission, which the administration billed as a programme “comparable in urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project” to accelerate US science with AI. At a summit on 22 July, officials announced about 280 winning projects in a first phase of the programme. Teams will apply AI to problems such as improving the US power grid and automating laboratories, and will receive a 9-month grant for between US$500,000 and $750,000. Researchers in these teams can also submit applications for a second phase: a three-year programme involving millions in annual funding.

“I was very, very, very happy” to be chosen “because it was incredibly competitive,” winner Jeremy Zucker told Nature at the summit. Zucker, a computational scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in Richland, Washington, is leading a project that will model algal growth in ponds to maximize biofuel production.

Kratsios’s report got a more mixed reception at a hearing in Washington DC that he attended on the same day. In the report, he calls for shifting US science funding away from “legacy institutions” such as universities. “Too much of our research enterprise has come to serve itself rather than the scientists within it,” he wrote. Under this new vision, individual scientists would be supported by programmes such as ‘golden tickets’, which give grant reviewers the ability to override the decisions of their colleagues to fund high-risk proposals. “We should be testing other ways to make breakthroughs than what we’ve been doing for so many years,” he said at the hearing of the US House of Representatives Committee on Science, Space and Technology. He argued that US science is stagnating and needs to be rethought.

Members of the US Congress, who decide what science to fund, had mixed reactions. Republicans on the committee broadly expressed support for Kratsios’s vision for US science; Democrats, however, criticized the Trump administration’s cuts to science budgets and agencies, as well as its push to take political control of grant awards. “You aren’t launching us into ‘the golden age of innovation’. You’re sending us back to the Stone Age,” said Gabe Amo, a Democrat representing Rhode Island.

Some scientists have been quick to criticize the report. Carl Bergstrom, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Washington in Seattle, wrote on the social-media platform Bluesky that the administration seems determined to “destroy” US universities. (Trump and his Republican allies have accused US research institutions of being discriminatory towards conservative views, and the administration has withheld funding from some universities, citing antisemitism.)

Grant challenges

Lawmakers also questioned Kratsios about media reports, including one from Nature, that the US National Science Foundation (NSF) plans to claw back about $500 million from its grant-making divisions and funnelling the money towards a new White House initiative. Democrat Zoe Lofgren of California queried the chief science adviser about this. He responded: “I’m not familiar with those details. I would refer you to NSF,” but made the case that the United States should “be more deliberative and specific about trying to tackle grand challenges”.

NSF plans cuts to core science programmes to fund White House initiative

Nature has learnt that the NSF has now pulled back $300 million from two of its divisions: mathematics and physical sciences, and computer and information science and engineering. Programme officers, who handle grant proposals at the NSF, have pulled back 150 proposals that have already passed peer review to free up the money, which was allotted to the agency by the US Congress. Some proposals have been rescinded, others have had funding cuts and still others have been held until the next fiscal year.

Staff members at the NSF, who spoke to Nature on the condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals, say the money is probably going to a programme called Grand Research Challenges, organized by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, which Kratsios runs. A preliminary document shown to Nature that appears to outline the challenges lists four areas: the future of intelligence, the frontier of quantum phenomena, advanced materials and matter and the foundations of biological design.

A spokesperson for the NSF said that the agency would not comment on internal budget deliberations. They said that funds for research activities in fiscal year 2026 could be awarded that year or the next one, and that "NSF revises budgets and manages portfolios as needed".

华盛顿特区

对于美国总统唐纳德·特朗普政府中的科学来说，这是重要的一周。 周二，总统首席科学顾问迈克尔·克拉齐奥斯 (Michael Kratsios) 发布了一份名为《科学：新黄金时代》的报告，建议对联邦政府资助的研究进行重大改变。 第二天，他帮助揭晓了创世任务（政府旗舰人工智能计划）研究经费的首批获奖者。

在过去的一年半里，共和党领导的政府因试图削减其不赞成的美国科学经费而成为头条新闻。 本周的事件值得注意，因为它们推动了它所青睐的科学——特别是人工智能。

特朗普拥有巨大的人工智能和量子野心：这位科学家的工作就是让它们成为现实

大约 5,000 个团队向 Genesis Mission 申请了资金，政府将其称为“与曼哈顿计划相当的紧迫性和雄心”的计划，旨在利用人工智能加速美国科学发展。 在 7 月 22 日的峰会上，官员们宣布了该计划第一阶段的约 280 个获奖项目。 团队将把人工智能应用于改善美国电网和自动化实验室等问题，并将获得为期 9 个月的 50 万美元至 75 万美元的资助。 这些团队的研究人员还可以提交第二阶段的申请：一个为期三年的项目，每年涉及数百万美元的资金。

获胜者杰里米·扎克在峰会上告诉《自然》杂志，“我非常、非常、非常高兴”被选中，“因为竞争非常激烈”。 扎克是华盛顿州里奇兰太平洋西北国家实验室的计算科学家，他正在领导一个项目，该项目将模拟池塘中的藻类生长，以最大限度地提高生物燃料的产量。

克雷西奥斯当天参加了在华盛顿特区举行的听证会，他的报告得到的评价褒贬不一。 在报告中，他呼吁将美国的科学经费从大学等“传统机构”上转移出来。 “我们的研究事业太多是为了自身服务，而不是为其中的科学家服务，”他写道。 在这一新愿景下，个别科学家将得到“金票”等计划的支持，这些计划使拨款审查者能够推翻同事的决定，为高风险提案提供资金。 他在美国众议院科学、空间和技术委员会的听证会上表示：“我们应该测试其他方法来取得突破，而不是我们多年来一直在做的事情。” 他认为美国科学正在停滞不前，需要重新思考。

决定资助哪些科学的美国国会议员反应不一。 委员会中的共和党人普遍表示支持克拉齐奥斯对美国科学的愿景；然而，民主党人批评特朗普政府削减科学预算和机构，以及推动对拨款的政治控制。 “你并没有让我们进入‘创新的黄金时代’。 你正在让我们回到石器时代，”代表罗德岛州的民主党人加布·阿莫说。

一些科学家很快就批评了这份报告。 西雅图华盛顿大学进化生物学家卡尔·伯格斯特罗姆在社交媒体平台“蓝天”上写道，政府似乎决心“摧毁”美国大学。 （特朗普及其共和党盟友指责美国研究机构歧视保守派观点，政府以反犹太主义为由扣留了一些大学的资助。）

赠款挑战

议员们还就包括《自然》杂志在内的媒体报道向克拉西奥斯提出质疑，称美国国家科学基金会 (NSF) 计划从其拨款部门收回约 5 亿美元，并将这笔资金用于一项新的白宫计划。 加利福尼亚州民主党人佐伊·洛夫格伦就此向首席科学顾问提出质询。 他回答说：“我不熟悉这些细节。 我建议你参考美国国家科学基金会（NSF）”，但他指出美国应该“更加审慎和具体地尝试应对重大挑战”。

美国国家科学基金会计划削减核心科学项目以资助白宫倡议

《自然》杂志获悉，美国国家科学基金会 (NSF) 现已从其两个部门撤回 3 亿美元：数学和物理科学以及计算机和信息科学与工程。 NSF 负责处理拨款提案的项目官员撤回了 150 项已通过同行评审的提案，以腾出美国国会分配给该机构的资金。 一些提案已被撤销，另一些提案已被削减资金，还有一些提案被搁置至下一财年。

美国国家科学基金会的工作人员因担心遭到报复而不愿透露姓名，他们表示这笔资金可能会用于一个名为“重大研究挑战”的项目，该项目由克拉齐奥斯负责的白宫科学技术政策办公室组织。 向《自然》杂志展示的一份初步文件似乎概述了这些挑战，列出了四个领域：智能的未来、量子现象的前沿、先进材料和物质以及生物设计的基础。

美国国家科学基金会发言人表示，该机构不会对内部预算审议发表评论。 他们表示，2026 财年的研究活动资金可能会在当年或下一年发放，并且“NSF 将根据需要修改预算并管理投资组合”。
